title: FP8 Precision & Microscaling (MX): How E4M3 and E5M2 Formats Double GPU Matrix Throughput Without Loss of Accuracy
summary: Scaling transformer training and inference across modern GPU clusters faces severe memory bandwidth and compute limitations. While 16-bit floating point (FP16 and BF16) has long been the standard, NVIDIA Hopper (H100) and Blackwell architectures introduced native FP8 Tensor Cores that double raw floating point operations per second (FLOPS) and cut memory traffic in half. However, compressing numbers into 8 bits requires balancing dynamic range against precision. By splitting representations into two distinct formats—E4M3 for forward activations and weights, and E5M2 for backward gradients—and applying block-level Microscaling (MX), systems achieve near-FP16 accuracy with 2x throughput.
analogyTitle: The Real-Life Analogy: The Pocket Ruler with Interchangeable Magnifying Glasses
analogy:
Imagine an architect who needs to sketch a 50-story skyscraper on a small pocket notebook.

Under FP16 / FP32 (The Full Drafting Table), the architect carries massive blueprints and heavy steel calipers. Every measurement is recorded to ten decimal places. It is ultra-accurate, but transporting the blueprints requires a pickup truck (memory bandwidth bottleck), and drawing each line takes twice as long.

Under FP8 with Microscaling (The Pocket Ruler with Micro-Lenses), the architect uses a compact 8-millimeter pocket ruler. For delicate interior plumbing, they click on a high-precision lens (E4M3: more mantissa bits for fine detail). For giant exterior structural beams, they switch to a wide-angle lens (E5M2: more exponent bits to cover huge numbers without clipping). In addition, every small 32-element section gets its own tiny scaling multiplier (Microscaling). The sketches take up 50% less paper, the drafting moves twice as fast, and the skyscraper stands perfectly straight without collapsing.

sections.heading: 1. The 8-Bit Floating Point Dilemma: Range vs. Precision
sections.content:
An 8-bit byte provides only 256 unique bit patterns. In contrast to integer quantization (INT8) which spaces values uniformly along a linear grid, floating-point formats divide bits into three segments:

• Sign bit ($S$): 1 bit indicating positive or negative.
• Exponent bits ($E$): Determines dynamic range (scale factor $2^{E - \text{bias}}$).
• Mantissa / Fraction bits ($M$): Determines precision (significant digits).

With only 7 bits remaining after the sign bit, engineers face an inescapable trade-off: allocating bits to the exponent expands dynamic range to prevent underflow and overflow, but robs bits from the mantissa, increasing rounding error and quantization noise.

sections.heading: 2. E4M3 vs. E5M2: Two Specialized Formats for Deep Learning
sections.content:
The IEEE FP8 standards consortium and NVIDIA resolved this trade-off by introducing two distinct FP8 formats:

• E4M3 (1 Sign, 4 Exponent, 3 Mantissa):
Offers higher precision with 3 mantissa bits (8 discrete steps between powers of two). Its dynamic range is limited (maximum representable value is 448). This format is ideal for forward activations and model weights, where values are normally distributed and outlier magnitude is bounded.

• E5M2 (1 Sign, 5 Exponent, 2 Mantissa):
Matches the dynamic range of BF16 (maximum value ~57,344) but retains only 2 bits of precision. This format is essential for backward gradients and optimizer states, where gradient magnitudes vary across orders of magnitude and clipping triggers training divergence.

Modern transformer engines dynamically cast tensors between E4M3 (GEMM input multiplication) and E5M2 (backward error accumulation), maintaining training stability without human intervention.

sections.heading: 3. Microscaling (MX) Formats: Overcoming Outliers at Scale
sections.content:
As models scale past 100 billion parameters, single activation channels frequently develop extreme outlier spikes that exceed standard tensor-wide FP8 scaling factors.

• Per-Tensor Scaling Flaws: In standard FP8, a single outlier forces the entire tensor's scale factor upward, pushing 99% of normal tokens into the lowest quantization bins where they suffer severe underflow.

• Microscaling (MX) Block Normalization: Standardized by the Open Compute Project (OCP), Microscaling divides tensors into small blocks of 32 elements. Each 32-element block shares an independent 8-bit scale factor (E8M0). If an outlier appears in block 4, only block 4 scales down; the remaining 31 blocks maintain high precision.

• Hardware Integration: Dedicated hardware decompression units in Hopper and Blackwell unpack MX blocks directly inside the Tensor Core register file at zero clock cycle latency penalty, unlocking 2x compute throughput in production inference servers.

takeaway: FP8 doubles GPU matrix multiply throughput by halving data movement across high-bandwidth memory. By deploying E4M3 for forward activations and E5M2 for backward gradients, coupled with 32-element Microscaling (MX) blocks, machine learning systems achieve the compute speed of 8-bit formats without sacrificing training stability.
